articleEn: On the evening of Saturday, 26 November 1977, at 5:10 p.m. GMT, many homes in southern England had their televisions on. ITN was running a news summary about the Rhodesian Bush War, the conflict in what is now Zimbabwe. Then the newsreader's voice suddenly vanished. A deep buzz replaced it, followed by a distorted male voice. The voice called itself Vrillon and claimed to be a representative of the Ashtar Galactic Command. It said that time was running short for Earth.

The message lasted about four minutes. In total, the interruption ran for roughly five and a half minutes, after which the broadcast returned to its schedule. On screen at that moment was a 1947 cartoon, The Goofy Gophers, and the evening went back to normal.

But where did the voice come from? Had someone really reached a signal powerful enough to take over television sets across several areas? Who did it, and how? And, most of all, has the incident ever been given a definitive answer?

This is the story of the Southern Television broadcast interruption. It involves technology, fear and a hoaxer who was never caught. Let's go back to that evening and see what was happening in southern England.

articleEn: Picture a November evening in 1977. People across southern England are watching news and programmes, and in this region they are watching Southern Television. The incident happened in parts of southern England, not across the whole of Britain. At 5:10 p.m. GMT, ITN's Ivor Mills was presenting a news summary on the latest developments in the Rhodesian Bush War. It was a routine bulletin, and Southern Television had no idea what was about to happen.

To understand the story, it helps to know how TV sound and pictures reach your home. A television transmitter is an electronic device that sends a video signal by radio waves, along with a synchronized audio channel. The waves reach the TV in your house, which turns them into picture and sound. Transmitters need a licence from the authorities. Their signals travel on VHF and UHF bands and move in line of sight, so reception is usually limited to about 40 to 60 miles.

The transmitter that matters here was the Hannington transmitter. It stood in northern Hampshire and was owned by the Independent Broadcasting Authority (IBA). Only viewers who received their TV sound from Hannington had their audio disrupted, so the effect was limited to one area. The sound changed into a deep buzz, and then a distorted male voice delivered a message for about four minutes.

Southern Television's own staff did not know it was happening. They found out only when viewers started calling. According to the IBA, it was the first interruption of its kind in the country. articleEn: So who is Ashtar? To answer that, we have to go back well before 1977. According to sources, the name Ashtar and the idea of an Ashtar Command are linked to claims of extraterrestrial communication from the 1950s. George Van Tassel is associated with them. He is described as a UFO contactee, someone who claims contact with beings from space. Van Tassel claimed he received a message from Ashtar. That was only a claim, not an established fact. Others then began saying they could channel the Ashtar Command, meaning they claimed to pass on its messages. Again, these are all claims, not proven facts.

Another source mentions Ashtar Sheran, described as an allegedly channeled alien said to command a fleet of flying saucers around Earth. By this claim, the being is active near our planet with a fleet. This is purely a claim and not a confirmed event.

The name Ashtar has other meanings too. Malik al-Ashtar was an Arab military commander who died in 658. A similar form of the name is used for the Ethiopian Aksumite god Attar. The video game Ninja Gaiden II also has a villain named Ashtar. These are different things, and the sources show no link between them and the Vrillon voice. They merely share a name.

Now to the message itself. Vrillon said people had seen them for years as lights in the sky. The message mentioned the Age of Aquarius, saying the planet was entering a new era that could be a time of peace and evolution. It also spoke of a great awakening, on the condition that humans learn to live in peace. It added that small groups around the world were learning peace and carrying forward the light of the coming age.

British newspapers of the time spelled the voice's name in different ways: Gillon, Ashdown Galactic Command, and Asteron. According to the original transcript, the name was Vrillon and the organization was the Ashtar Galactic Command. This difference matters later in the story. But if Ashtar was an old claim, who turned it into a TV voice in 1977, and how did it reach so many people?

articleEn: Let's first hear what the voice actually said, because the full transcript still exists. The message began with an introduction. The voice said this was Vrillon, a representative of the Ashtar Galactic Command, speaking to the listeners. It said that for years you have seen us as lights in the sky, and now we speak to you with peace and wisdom. Then came a warning: they had come to alert people to the future of their race and world, so that they could avoid disaster.

Next the Age of Aquarius was mentioned. The message said this could be a time of peace, but only if the rulers were aware of the forces of evil. The tone then hardened. The voice said to listen in silence, or you may not get another chance. All weapons of evil must be removed. The time for conflict was said to be over. If humans proved themselves worthy, they could reach the next stages of their evolution. Time was short, and people had to learn very soon how to live together in peace and goodwill. The message said people were free to accept or reject the teachings of the small groups, but only those who learned peace would reach the next spiritual levels.

The voice then repeated its name, Vrillon, representative of the Ashtar Galactic Command, and immediately gave another warning. Many false prophets and false leaders were active in the world, it said, and people should beware of them. They would drain your energy, which you call money, and give you worthless things in return. Instead, listeners were told to pay attention to the divine voice within, which would protect them and help them tell truth from confusion. This voice of truth lay within each person, and listening to it would put them on the path of evolution.

At the end, the tone softened. The voice said they had watched humanity grow for years, and that people had seen their lights in the sky. It claimed there are many more beings on and around Earth than scientists accept, and said there was no need to be afraid. Listeners were told to know themselves and live in harmony with the ways of their Earth. The voice promised to do what it could to help. The message closed with the words that they were now leaving the planes of the listeners' existence, and with a blessing of the cosmic love and truth of the universe.

One account says the message lasted about four minutes, while another says that after five and a half minutes the broadcast returned to its normal programme. This is the full transcript, but the newspapers reported it in different ways. Next we will see who wrote what.

articleEn: Then, suddenly, the voice stopped. The message was complete, and the interruption ended. Consider the timing: the ITN news summary began at 5:10 p.m. GMT, and within a few minutes everything had changed. According to sources, the broadcast went back to its scheduled programme, a 1947 cartoon called The Goofy Gophers. A moment earlier a voice had been talking about Earth's future, and now cartoon characters were on screen. For families sitting at home, it must have been a strange moment. The sources say that hundreds of people phoned later. There is a small confusion too: some places call the cartoon Looney Tunes and others Merrie Melodies, but both refer to the same 1947 cartoon.

The oddest part is that Southern Television itself did not know anything had gone wrong with its broadcast. The station learned of it only when viewers began phoning. So the news reached homes first and the station later. When the cartoon ended, Southern Television apologised, saying some viewers had experienced interference with the sound. This disruption affected only viewers whose TV sound signal came from the Hannington transmitter, which meant only parts of southern England.

That night ITN also reported the incident, in its late-evening bulletin on Saturday. It is interesting that ITN was the same organization giving the news summary when the interruption happened, and now it was making the interruption into news. The Independent Broadcasting Authority said something important: this was the first interruption of its kind in the country. So this was not just one strange evening.

At this point the picture looks like this: a short message, a cartoon, hundreds of confused viewers and no clear answer. The question became what it takes to change a broadcast's sound. The answer was technical, and we will come to it. First, if the station did not know, what did people do? And what did the newspapers write over the following days?

articleEn: Now to people's reactions. After the incident, Southern Television received hundreds of phone calls from worried viewers. The calls did not stop at the TV station. Winchester police also received calls, and people dialled the emergency number 999, the UK's emergency line. They used it to report the incident, so for some people this was not simply a joke. According to sources, the incident caused some alarm locally. Southern Television received hundreds of calls and Winchester police more than 50. Both figures show the unease that followed.

The story then spread. American newspapers also printed it, and many took it from United Press International and the Associated Press. So an evening in southern England became world news. But as the story spread, details changed. Both British and American papers ran it, and no two reports were the same.

The first problem was the name. The transcript says Vrillon, but most British papers wrote Gillon or Asteron. One wrote Gillon of the Ashdown Galactic Command, so not only the name changed but the organization's name went from Ashtar to Ashdown. The difference seems small, but it shows that several versions of one event were circulating. Reports were sometimes contradictory. The IBA said this was the first such incident in the country, and it is possible that is why everyone told the story as they understood it, though that is only a guess.

The words of the message were disputed as well. Some papers wrote that the voice threatened a swift attack on Earth unless weapons were put down. Other reports, based on the United Press International report, said the voice said Earth would have to leave the galaxy if it did not learn peace. But the transcript we have mentions neither an attack nor leaving the galaxy. It talks about removing weapons and learning peace.

One person questioned this reporting. On 6 December 1977, Sir John Whitmore spoke on British commercial radio. He said the message was not threatening or frightening, and that this may have been the newspapers' own projection. A caution is needed here: Whitmore's view was his opinion, but by reading the transcript we can see for ourselves that the message contained both warning and peace.

There is a lesson in this debate. When an event spreads quickly, the original transcript and the newspaper summary can differ. That is why we played the whole message. So three versions were circulating: one of peace, one of invasion and one of leaving the galaxy. Amid this confusion the biggest question remained. Where did the voice actually come from, and had someone really done something?

articleEn: Three bodies began investigating the incident: the police, the Post Office, and the Independent Broadcasting Authority (IBA), which owned the transmitter. The Post Office had legal powers under the 1949 Wireless Telegraphy Act to control radio frequencies, which is why it was involved.

First, what does a television transmitter do? It is an electronic device that carries picture and sound to viewers by radio waves. Each transmitter needs a government licence and is limited to a specific frequency channel and power level. VHF and UHF waves travel in line of sight, so reception is usually only 40 to 60 miles. A transmitter's effective strength is its output power multiplied by antenna gain, which is called ERP.

Now the key point. The Hannington transmitter worked in an unusual way. It was one of a few large transmitters that took their signal off the air. It did not get a direct feed by landline. Instead it picked up the IBA's Rowridge transmitter signal off-air and rebroadcast it. Rowridge was on the Isle of Wight. So Hannington's receiver caught a signal from far away and passed it on.

Now imagine a small transmitter placed very close to that receiver. This became the basic explanation of the incident. Even a low-power signal, if very near the receiver, can overpower the real signal. This can be called a capture effect. Hannington then amplified the wrong signal and spread it over a wide area, so one small action reached many homes.

A Southern Television spokesman confirmed this explanation. According to him, a hoaxer in North Hampshire placed a second transmitter very close and overrode the signal. The IBA said such a hoax needed considerable technical know-how, so real technical skill was behind it. If those responsible had been caught, they could have faced a fine of up to 200 pounds under the Wireless Telegraphy Act. Remember, Southern Television itself did not know its signal had been hijacked and learned from viewers' calls.

So what did the investigation conclude? One thing was clear: the voice came not from a spacecraft but from a small unauthorised transmitter on the ground. Another interesting point is that the IBA said an interruption of this kind was the first of its nature in the country.

There is also a difference in the figures. Sources say the message lasted about four minutes, while the whole interruption was put at about five and a half minutes. This tells us the technical weakness was at a single point: a receiver that passed on the wrong audio as if it were genuine. In a TV transmitter the audio and video input stages are separate, and in this incident only the audio was replaced. Audio is usually frequency modulated (FM), while video uses amplitude modulation. The two are combined at the end and broadcast from the antenna.
So, in short, there was no mysterious alien technology behind the voice, only a weakness in how the radio system was arranged. But who did it?

articleEn: On 30 November, Southern Television told the press that it knew how the interruption had happened and had closed the loophole. So only four days after the event, the station claimed the route had been shut. But there was no trace of the person who did it. By December a Home Office spokesperson said the investigations were complete, although no one had been caught. Another Southern Television statement said the chance of catching the culprit was very slim unless the same person did it again.

Think about that. The investigations were declared complete, but the person behind the voice was not caught. The story stopped there. Meanwhile, an IBA engineer said that in future the tower could be protected from such incidents. One more point: the Wireless Telegraphy Act had a penalty, but since nobody was caught, no one was ever fined.

Now to UFO circles. The Aetherius Society, a UFO religious group, investigated the incident. Its conclusion was that it was a hoax. So even a UFO group did not consider the message genuine. Even so, some people accepted the broadcast at face value, and the incident became a footnote in ufology.

Time passed and the story changed. By 1985 the incident had become urban folklore, and some people said it had never been explained. In reality an explanation existed. The story of the Hannington transmitter and an unauthorised nearby transmitter was on record. That is the difference worth noticing: by 1985 some were saying there was no explanation, while the investigation had already produced one.

In 1999 an episode of the children's television series It's a Mystery retold the incident with faux news reports. It showed viewers watching the event at home. Interestingly, it was made by Meridian Broadcasting, which was among Southern's successor organizations.

One important point is that our sources record no name, motive or group for the hoaxer. So we cannot accuse anyone. We only know that technical know-how was needed, and that whoever did it exploited a weak point. So can an investigation that was completed have told us everything? The explanation existed, but the name and motive remained missing.
